questions.question: What is the essential difference between "interception before execution" and "after-the-fact rollback"?
options: Interception requires manual action; rollback executes automatically
Rollback always has cases it cannot recover (e.g. the email has already been read), while pre-execution interception costs nothing when it fires
The two are completely equivalent — just different names
questions.explanation: See the "The interception point is before execution" section: rollback always has unrecoverable cases (the email already read), while pre-execution interception fires at zero cost — that is the essential difference between a gate and after-the-fact rollback.

questions.question: Designing "repeatedly approved same-class actions" as an evolution signal on the allow-list delivers what engineering value?
options: It automatically removes the action from the allow-list
Repeated approvals signal that the action should be added to the allow-list; repeated rejections signal the prompt or task definition is wrong
It triggers a human review that rejects all subsequent same-class requests
It auto-generates a new audit rule
questions.explanation: See the "Rejection is also input" section: the same action class approved repeatedly is a signal to allow-list it; rejected repeatedly is a signal that the prompt or task definition is wrong — approval data is itself evaluation material.

questions.question: In the defense-in-depth combo, the approval gate specifically guards against which class of risk?
questions.explanation: See the "The gate inside the defense-in-depth combo" section: guardrails block content risk, the gate (this lesson) blocks action risk, evaluation blocks quality risk — the three cover different failure surfaces, and the gate's position is action risk.
